title: Atmosphere
tagline: The composition and structure of the atmosphere, the heating that drives its motion, and the pressure systems and winds that follow.

overview.intro: The atmosphere is a thin envelope of gases held by gravity, and it is the medium in which weather happens. Solar radiation arrives unevenly, the land and sea heat at different rates, and the resulting differences in pressure set air in motion. This unit covers the composition of the atmosphere and why it varies with height, the layers from troposphere to exosphere, the processes by which the atmosphere is heated and temperature varies with latitude, altitude and season, and the pressure belts, planetary winds and local breezes that make up the circulation of the lower atmosphere.

facts.value: Troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere and exosphere.

facts.label: Pressure belts

learningOutcomes: State the composition of the atmosphere and its variation with height.

learn.title: Composition and structure of the atmosphere

blocks.text: Dry air near the surface is a mixture of gases: nitrogen about 78 per cent by volume, oxygen about 21 per cent, argon about 0.9 per cent, carbon dioxide about 0.04 per cent, and traces of other gases. Water vapour varies from almost nothing in polar air to several per cent in the tropics, and it is the most variable and most important component for weather because it carries latent heat and forms clouds. Dust and smoke provide the nuclei on which water vapour condenses. With height the composition stays uniform up to about 80 kilometres, since gases mix turbulently, but total pressure falls rapidly because the mass of air above decreases.

learn.title: Heating of the atmosphere and temperature variation

blocks.text: The atmosphere is heated in three ways: by conduction, which is direct contact between the ground and the air above it; by convection, in which warmed air rises and is replaced by cooler air; and by radiation, which is the principal method. The sun radiates short waves that pass through the atmosphere with little absorption, the land absorbs them and re-radiates long terrestrial radiation, and it is this long-wave radiation that atmospheric gases such as carbon dioxide and water vapour absorb. The atmosphere is therefore heated from below, which is why temperature normally falls with height through the troposphere.

Temperature varies with latitude because the angle of the sun’s rays and the length of day differ, falling from the equator toward the poles. It varies with altitude because of the decrease in pressure, rising over land in summer and falling with height at roughly 6.5 degrees Celsius per kilometre. It varies with season through the changing angle and duration of sunshine, and locally with cloud cover, which reflects radiation by day and traps it at night.

items.note: Water has a higher specific heat, so it warms and cools slowly and moderates the air above it.

blocks.text: Unequal heating produces a belt of low pressure near the equator, where intense heating makes air rise, and high pressure near the poles, where cold dense air sinks. Between them sit subtropical highs around 30 degrees, formed where cooled air that rose at the equator descends, and subpolar lows near 60 degrees, formed where rising air meets polar air. The movement of air from high to low pressure, deflected by the Earth’s rotation, gives the planetary winds: the trade winds between the subtropical highs and the equator, the westerlies between the subtropical and subpolar belts, and the polar easterlies at high latitudes.

blocks.caption: Global pressure belts and their winds
rows: Rising air, light variable winds, heavy convectional rain
Steady easterlies, from subtropical high toward the equator
Descending dry air, calm conditions, many deserts
Prevailing south-westerlies in the northern hemisphere
Rising air, cyclonic storms and variable weather
Cold dry winds blowing from the polar high

blocks.text: The deflection that shapes these winds is the Coriolis force, which arises because a rotating body carries moving objects sideways relative to the surface. It acts to the right in the northern hemisphere and to the left in the southern, it is zero at the equator and greatest at the poles, and it is why winds spiral rather than blow straight from high to low pressure.

learn.title: Local winds: land and sea, mountain and valley

blocks.text: Local breezes arise where heating differs over short distances. During the day the land heats faster than the sea, air above it rises, and cooler air from over the sea flows in to replace it, giving a sea breeze from afternoon to evening. At night the land cools faster, the pressure over it rises, and a land breeze blows from the shore to the sea. In mountainous country, a valley slope cools quickly at night and dense cold air drains downslope as a katabatic wind, while by day the sunlit slope heats the air above it which rises as an anabatic wind up the valley.

keyPoints: Air is about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, with argon, carbon dioxide and variable water vapour.
Water vapour is the most variable component and the driver of weather.
The atmosphere is layered into troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere and exosphere.
All weather occurs in the troposphere, where temperature falls with height.
The atmosphere is heated mainly from below by terrestrial radiation.
Temperature falls with latitude and altitude and varies with season and continentality.
Equatorial heating produces low pressure; polar cooling produces high pressure.
The Coriolis force deflects moving air to the right in the northern hemisphere and left in the southern.
Trade winds, westerlies and polar easterlies fill the gaps between the pressure belts.
Land and sea breezes and mountain winds arise from differential heating over short distances.
examFocus: Pressure belt diagrams should show belts and winds together with their latitudes, since half the marks are for position.
Heating questions must state that the atmosphere is heated from below and explain why temperature falls with height.

questions.prompt: The layer of the atmosphere in which all weather occurs is:
questions.explanation: The troposphere holds nearly all the water vapour and dust of the atmosphere, so clouds, rain and storms are confined to it.

questions.prompt: The atmosphere is heated mainly by:
options: Long-wave terrestrial radiation absorbed by atmospheric gases
questions.answer: Long-wave terrestrial radiation absorbed by atmospheric gases
questions.explanation: Solar short waves pass through the atmosphere and warm the surface, which re-radiates long waves that the gases absorb, so heating happens from below.

questions.prompt: The subtropical high pressure belt near 30 degrees latitude is associated with:
options: Descending dry air and many of the world’s deserts
questions.answer: Descending dry air and many of the world’s deserts
questions.explanation: Air that rose at the equator cools and descends near 30 degrees, producing dry, stable conditions in which deserts commonly form.

questions.prompt: A sea breeze blows from sea to land because:
options: The sea warms faster than the land by day
The land warms faster by day, so air rises over it and cooler air moves in from the sea
The sea has higher pressure at night
Winds are deflected by the Coriolis force alone
questions.answer: The land warms faster by day, so air rises over it and cooler air moves in from the sea
questions.explanation: Differential heating is the cause: the faster-heating land lowers pressure over it and draws air seaward-to-landward replacement.

questions.prompt: The three main gases of the atmosphere by volume are nitrogen, oxygen and __________ .
questions.explanation: Argon makes up about 0.9 per cent of dry air, while carbon dioxide, though vital, is present only in trace amounts of about 0.04 per cent.

questions.prompt: The apparent deflection of moving air caused by the rotation of the Earth is called the __________ force.
questions.explanation: The deflection is to the right in the northern hemisphere and to the left in the southern, and it is why winds spiral around pressure systems.

questions.prompt: State four layers of the atmosphere in order from the surface.
questions.answer: Four layers in order are the troposphere, extending to about 12 kilometres and holding all the weather; the stratosphere, extending to about 50 kilometres and containing the ozone layer; the mesosphere, extending to about 80 kilometres and containing the coldest temperatures; and the thermosphere, extending to about 800 kilometres, where temperature rises sharply through absorption of short-wave radiation. The exosphere lies above it.
questions.explanation: The order matters as much as the names, and one characteristic for each layer earns the remaining marks.

questions.prompt: Explain why temperature falls with height in the troposphere.
questions.answer: The atmosphere is heated from below rather than from above: solar short-wave radiation passes through the air and is absorbed by the land and sea, which re-radiate it as long-wave terrestrial radiation, and it is this long-wave radiation that the gases of the atmosphere absorb. Because the source of heat is at the surface, the air nearest the ground is warmest, and air further from the surface receives less energy and is cooler. Pressure and density also fall with height, so the thin air absorbs less radiation, and temperature therefore declines at about 6.5 degrees Celsius per kilometre through the troposphere.
questions.explanation: The answer must trace the path of energy from the sun to the surface to the air, since that chain is what explains the gradient.

questions.prompt: Describe the global pressure belts and the planetary winds that blow between them.
questions.answer: Unequal heating of the globe produces a belt of equatorial low pressure near the equator, where intense heating makes air rise, and polar high pressure at high latitudes, where cold dense air sinks. Air that rises at the equator cools and descends near 30 degrees, creating subtropical highs, while near 60 degrees air rising from the meeting of warmer and colder masses creates subpolar lows. The winds that result are the trade winds, blowing from the subtropical highs toward the equatorial low as steady easterlies; the westerlies, blowing from the subtropical highs poleward toward the subpolar lows; and the polar easterlies, blowing from the polar high toward the subpolar low. Each wind is deflected by the Coriolis force, to the right in the northern hemisphere and to the left in the southern, which is why the trades in the northern hemisphere come from the north-east and the westerlies from the south-west. Between the trades lies the equatorial doldrums of light variable wind, and between the trades and westerlies at about 30 degrees lie the horse latitudes of calm descending air.
questions.explanation: Full marks need the belts with approximate latitudes, the winds between them, and the role of the deflection force.

questions.prompt: A city on a plain records 38°C at 3 pm and 11°C before dawn in the same week, while a coastal town 60 km away records 27°C and 18°C. Explain both the daily range and the coastal difference using the physics of heating.
questions.answer: The inland city shows a large diurnal range because land has a low specific heat, so it heats quickly under daytime radiation and cools quickly at night by terrestrial radiation with little cloud or moisture to slow the loss. The coastal town shows a small range because water has a much higher specific heat, absorbing heat slowly during the day and releasing it slowly at night, and because evaporation from the sea consumes energy that would otherwise raise the temperature. The same principle explains the coastal difference: the sea breeze of the afternoon imports cooler marine air over the town, capping its daytime maximum, while at night the land breeze and the moderating water keep the minimum higher. Latitude, altitude and season are effectively the same in both places, so the difference must come from the surface and its heating properties, together with the circulation the heating sets up. Coastal areas therefore have a marine climate of small range while inland areas show continentality with a large range.
questions.explanation: Marks are for identifying specific heat and evaporation as the mechanism, then using the same mechanism for both the daily range and the difference between the two towns.
